953.title: Aurobindo (selections)
953.hook: a prisoner looks at the bars of his cell and sees Krishna
953.howItsDone: Some followers of Sri Aurobindo read his speeches, letters and books as part of daily practice, and his ashram in Puducherry and centers elsewhere hold collective meditation and study of his writings.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ramana Maharshi's shade: happiness isn't in things, and the wise one stays out of the sun. Did you catch the quiet after a want was met? Day nine hundred fifty-three.

A jail cell in Calcutta, and a prisoner waiting for his trial. He'd been a writer and a political leader, arguing hard for India's freedom from British rule, and now he's accused in a bombing case. He's allowed very little. One of the few things he has is a copy of the Bhagavad Gita. Later, after he walked out free, he gave a speech about what happened to him in that cell. His name was Aurobindo Ghose. People came to know him as Sri Aurobindo.
screen: `A CELL IN CALCUTTA.` → `A TRIAL, AND A GITA.` → `A SPEECH, AFTER RELEASE.`

segments.voice: In the speech, Aurobindo says he had asked God for guidance before his arrest, and in jail he felt the answer came. He was given the Gita, and he was asked, as he tells it, to live what it teaches, not just read it. Then something changed in how he saw. He looked at the walls that held him, and they were no longer walls. It was Vasudeva, a name for Krishna, standing around him. He walked under the branches of the tree in the yard, and it was Vasudeva. He looked at the bars of the cell, the grating on the door, and saw Vasudeva again. He looked at the other prisoners, thieves and men accused of murder, and he says he found Vasudeva in them too. Even in court, he says, when he looked at the magistrate and the prosecutor, he saw the same presence. Hold that up next to the Gita you read in an earlier year. In the Gita, Krishna tells Arjuna that the one who sees him in everything, and everything in him, is never lost to him. Aurobindo is describing what it was like when that line stopped being an idea. Notice where it happened. Not in a temple, not on a mountain. In a jail, among thieves and accused men. Keep that cell in mind for the next two days. In his account, the divine wasn't somewhere else, waiting for him to leave the world. It was there, in the bars and the faces. Tomorrow, the short sentence he built a whole yoga on.
screen: `IN JAIL, HE WAS GIVEN THE GITA.` · `THE WALLS, THE TREE, THE BARS: VASUDEVA.` · `EVEN IN THE PRISONERS AND THE COURT.` · then, large: `NOT ELSEWHERE: THERE, IN THE CELL.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let your eyes rest on something ordinary in front of you: a wall, a window frame, a cup. Look at it slowly. Then let your attention move to the next thing, and the next, without rushing. If you pray, you can hold each one in that prayer as Aurobindo held the walls of his cell, as a place where God might be. If you don't, simply give each thing the kind of attention you'd give to something precious. Last, bring to mind one person you find hard, and hold them there too. The bell holds the time.
Aurobindo. The writer and freedom fighter who, by his own account, saw Krishna in the walls, the bars and the prisoners of his jail.

Your line: Aurobindo, selections. Today, pick one place you'd rather not be, a waiting room, a commute, a dull meeting, and look at it once the way he looked at his cell. Day nine hundred fifty-three.

954.title: Aurobindo (selections)
954.hook: four words that bring yoga out of the cave and into the kitchen
954.howItsDone: Those who follow Sri Aurobindo's integral yoga try to bring work, relationships and study into their practice, often offering daily tasks to the divine; Auroville and the Pondicherry ashram organize community life around this idea.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Aurobindo in his cell, seeing Vasudeva in the walls, the bars and the other prisoners. Did you look at one unwanted place differently? Day nine hundred fifty-four.

A lone figure in a cave, far from traffic and bills and family arguments: that's one old picture of a yogi, sitting still while the rest of the world gets on with its errands. Holiness over there, ordinary life over here. Aurobindo, after his release, left politics behind and settled in Pondicherry, in the south, to give himself to yoga. But the yoga he taught there refused that split. He put it in a sentence of four words.
screen: `THE YOGI IN THE CAVE.` → `HOLINESS THERE, LIFE HERE.` → `A SENTENCE OF FOUR WORDS.`

segments.voice: The sentence comes from The Synthesis of Yoga, the book where Aurobindo sets out his way. It reads: all life is yoga. Not some of life. Not the quiet hour before work. All of it. The washing up, the job, the argument, the walk home. Here's how he gets there. The word synthesis means bringing things together, and that's what the book does. Take three roads the Gita speaks of: karma, the yoga of work; bhakti, the yoga of love; jnana, the yoga of knowledge. Aurobindo doesn't make anyone choose one. He gathers them into a single practice, so that working, loving and understanding all become ways of turning toward the divine. He calls this integral yoga. Then he goes a step further. Some paths, he says, aim to rise out of the world, to escape it. His aim is for the divine to come down into it and change it: the body, the mind, ordinary life, all made new. That's what he means when he writes about a divine life. Yesterday's cell sits underneath this. If Vasudeva can stand in prison walls, then there's no part of life too low or too dull to be part of the yoga. Other Hindu teachers and traditions read the goal differently, some as release from the world, some as union with God beyond it. Aurobindo's voice is one in that long conversation, and his particular word to it was this: don't leave. Bring it all in. Tomorrow, how he told that hope through an old story you already know.
screen: `ALL LIFE IS YOGA.` · `WORK, LOVE, KNOWLEDGE: GATHERED INTO ONE.` · `NOT ESCAPING THE WORLD, CHANGING IT.` · then, large: `DON'T LEAVE. BRING IT ALL IN.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably, and let the breath settle. Bring to mind the next ordinary thing you'll do after this: a chore, a message to answer, a meal to make. See yourself doing it, step by step, slowly. Now see it again, but as part of your practice, not a break from it. If you pray, you can offer that ordinary task in your own words. If you don't, simply decide to give it your whole attention. Rest with that picture. The bell holds the time.
Aurobindo. The teacher of integral yoga, who wrote that all life is yoga, and gathered work, love and knowledge into one way.
Your line: Aurobindo, selections. Today, choose one chore you usually rush, and do it as if it were part of the practice, because, in his words, all life is yoga. Day nine hundred fifty-four.

955.title: Aurobindo (selections)
955.hook: an old story you already know, retold as a legend and a symbol
955.howItsDone: Some followers of Sri Aurobindo read Savitri aloud, a few lines at a time, as a daily spiritual reading, and study groups at his ashram and centers read it together.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Aurobindo's four words: all life is yoga, with work, love and knowledge gathered into one. Which chore did you bring into the practice? Day nine hundred fifty-five.

A princess named Savitri chooses Satyavan for her husband, though she's told he will die within the year. On the day it comes, they're in the forest together, he lays his head in her lap, and Death himself arrives to carry him off. And Savitri gets up and follows Death. Earlier this year you heard that story as the Mahabharata tells it. Aurobindo heard something more in it, and turned it into a long poem of his own.
screen: `SAVITRI CHOOSES SATYAVAN.` → `DEATH COMES TO THE FOREST.` → `SHE GETS UP AND FOLLOWS.`

segments.voice: He called the poem Savitri, and gave it a subtitle: a legend and a symbol. In a short note at its front, he explains. The Mahabharata tells the tale, he says, as a story of married love that conquers death. He doesn't deny that. But he reads each person in it as standing for something larger too. Satyavan is the soul that carries the divine truth inside it, but has come down into the grip of death and ignorance. Savitri is the divine Word, daughter of the Sun, come down to be born and to save. Her father, the king who prayed so long for a child, stands for tapasya, the long, concentrated human effort that reaches up from the mortal toward the immortal. And Death, read this way, is more than the god who walks off with one young man. Some readers hear in him everything in the world that says this is how things are, nothing can change. Put that next to yesterday. If all life is yoga, and the aim is for the divine to come down and change life rather than leave it, then Savitri is that hope told as a story. She doesn't climb out of the world to escape death. She walks after Death, argues with him, and won't let go until life is given back. Aurobindo's reading doesn't replace the Mahabharata's. The old tale still stands, a wife's courage and a husband returned. He simply holds a second lamp up to it. A story can be what happened in a forest, and a picture of what happens in a soul.
screen: `A LEGEND AND A SYMBOL.` · `SATYAVAN: THE SOUL, HELD BY DEATH.` · `SAVITRI: THE DIVINE WORD, COME TO SAVE.` · then, large: `SHE WALKS AFTER DEATH.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. Bring to mind one thing in your life that feels fixed, a habit, a hurt, a situation that seems as if it can never change. Don't argue with it yet. Just see it clearly, the way Savitri saw Death standing in the forest. Then, with each breath, take one small step after it, in your mind, without letting go. You don't need to win anything right now. Only keep walking. If you pray, you can carry it into prayer with you. The bell holds the time.
Aurobindo. The teacher who retold Savitri as a legend and a symbol: the soul held by death, and the divine come down to bring it back to life.
Your line: Aurobindo, selections. Today, when you hear yourself say that's just how it is, picture Savitri getting up, and take one small step after it. Day nine hundred fifty-five.

956.title: Gandhi's Gita
956.hook: a young law student is embarrassed to admit he hasn't read the Gita
956.howItsDone: In Gandhian ashrams the closing verses of the Gita's second chapter, on the one of steady wisdom, are recited as part of daily prayer, and some Hindus learn Gita verses by heart, a few at a time.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Aurobindo's Savitri, a legend and a symbol: the soul held by death, and Savitri walking after Death until life is given back. Did you take one small step after something stuck? Day nine hundred fifty-six.

London, and a young Indian law student far from home. Two brothers he's met, Theosophists interested in Indian thought, are reading the Bhagavad Gita in an English translation, Edwin Arnold's verse version, and they invite him to read the original with them. And the young man has to admit something awkward. He has never read it. Not in Sanskrit, not in his own Gujarati. He tells this story about himself later, in his autobiography, and he says he felt ashamed. The young man was Mohandas Gandhi.
screen: `A LAW STUDENT IN LONDON.` → `TWO BROTHERS AND A GITA.` → `HE HAD NEVER READ IT.`

segments.voice: So Gandhi's Gita begins in an unlikely place: with friends from another country, an English verse translation, and a Sanskrit text he could only half follow. He reads it with them, and some verses near the end of the second chapter strike him hard. They trace a slide, step by step. A person dwells on the things the senses want. From dwelling comes attachment. From attachment, desire. From desire, anger. From anger, confusion. Memory slips, judgment fails, and the person is lost. Gandhi doesn't say he understood all of it then. But he says the book stayed with him, and he came to prize it above other books for knowing truth. Later, in South Africa, he did something very ordinary with it. He wrote verses out on slips of paper and stuck them on the wall where he washed in the morning, and learned them by heart while he went about getting ready for the day. Not in a temple. Next to the washbasin. Those verses at the end of chapter two describe a person the Gita calls sthitaprajna, the one whose wisdom stands steady, who isn't thrown about by every want and every fear. The verses about the steady one became part of the daily prayers in the community he founded. Notice the shape of this. Gandhi didn't arrive with the Gita already in hand, inherited and settled. He came to it a little late, a little embarrassed, and then he kept it close. Tomorrow, the bigger puzzle: how a man known for nonviolence read a book that opens on a battlefield.
screen: `A BORROWED BOOK, READ WITH FRIENDS.` · `DWELLING, ATTACHMENT, DESIRE, ANGER.` · `VERSES ON SLIPS BY THE WASHBASIN.` · then, large: `THE ONE WHOSE WISDOM STANDS STEADY.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably, and let the breath settle. Bring to mind one small want that has been tugging at you today: a snack, a scroll, a purchase, a reply you'd like to send. Watch the slide the Gita describes, slowly: the dwelling, the pull of it, the wanting. Don't scold yourself. Just see each step. Then let the attention rest on the breath, steady, the way the steady one in the Gita stays still while the wants come and go. If you pray, you can hold that steadiness in prayer. The bell holds the time.
Gandhi's Gita. The book Gandhi first read as a student in London, with friends, and then kept close, with verses stuck up beside the washbasin.
Your line: Gandhi's Gita. Today, write one line that matters to you on a slip of paper and put it where you wash in the morning. Day nine hundred fifty-six.

957.title: Gandhi's Gita
957.hook: a book that opens on a battlefield, read by a man of nonviolence
957.howItsDone: Readers of Gandhi's Anasakti Yoga often read the Gita's battle as a picture of the struggle within, and some Hindus keep a short daily reading of the Gita alongside their prayers.

segments.voice: Yesterday Gandhi's Gita began with a law student in London who admitted he had never read it, and later learned its verses by the washbasin. Did a line find its way onto your wall? Day nine hundred fifty-seven.

Two armies face each other on an open field. Conch shells sound across the lines. A warrior named Arjuna asks his charioteer to drive out into the gap between them, and he looks across and sees teachers, uncles, cousins, old friends. His bow slips from his hand. That is where the Bhagavad Gita begins: at the edge of a war, with the weapons about to be loosed. So here is a puzzle. Gandhi, the man the world knew for nonviolence, kept this book close and called it a guide for his life. How does a man of peace live by a book set on a battlefield? Today, his answer.
screen: `TWO ARMIES, ONE GAP BETWEEN THEM.` → `ARJUNA'S BOW SLIPS.` → `A MAN OF PEACE, A BOOK OF WAR?`

segments.voice: Gandhi made his own version of the Gita in Gujarati and called it Anasakti Yoga. In its introduction he says plainly that he did not read the war as history. He read the field as the human heart. The two armies, in his reading, are the forces of good and evil inside one person, and the battle is the one each of us fights there, day after day. Krishna, the charioteer, is for him the dweller within, the voice that speaks from the inside. So when Krishna tells Arjuna to stand up and fight, Gandhi hears something like this: don't run from the struggle inside you. Face it. Notice what that does to the book. A text that seems, on its surface, to send a man into battle becomes, in Gandhi's hands, a handbook for a nonviolent life. He went further. He wrote that, after years of trying to live the Gita's teaching, he had found that its kind of complete selflessness is not possible without nonviolence. It's fair to say clearly that this is one reading among several. Other readers, traditional commentators among them, take the war as a real war and Arjuna's duty as a warrior's real duty: Krishna is telling a soldier to do what his role asks, without hatred and without clinging to victory. Still others hold both at once, a real field and a mirror of the inner one. The Gita's own first line gives every reader something to work with. It names the place twice: dharmakshetra, kurukshetra. The field of dharma, the field of the Kurus. Read Gandhi's way, that first name carries the weight. The field of right living, on his reading, was not somewhere far away in an old story. It was the ground between what a person wants to do and what that person knows is right.
screen: `HE READ THE FIELD AS THE HEART.` · `KRISHNA: THE DWELLER WITHIN.` · `ONE READING AMONG SEVERAL.` · `THE FIELD OF DHARMA, THE FIELD OF THE KURUS.` · then, large: `THE BATTLE IS INSIDE.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath slow down on its own. Bring to mind one small battle you're in right now. Not a war, just a pull. Something you want to say and suspect you shouldn't, or something you know is right and keep putting off. Don't try to settle it yet. Just do what Arjuna did: drive out into the gap between the two lines and look at both sides, calmly. On the in-breath, see the side that pulls. On the out-breath, see the side that asks. If you pray, you can hold the whole field before Krishna, or before the one you pray to, without choosing yet. The bell holds the time.
Gandhi's Gita. The Bhagavad Gita as Gandhi read it: a battle fought inside the heart, with Krishna as the voice within.

Your line: Gandhi's Gita. Today, when you feel two pulls inside you, name it quietly to yourself, here's the field, and then choose the side you'd want to have chosen tonight. Day nine hundred fifty-seven.

958.title: Gandhi's Gita
958.hook: the word Gandhi put on the cover: anasakti
958.howItsDone: Some who follow the Gita's path of action try to offer their daily work without clinging to its results, and some readers of Gandhi pair Gita 2:47 with his line that means and ends are like seed and tree.

segments.voice: Yesterday in Gandhi's Gita, the battlefield moved inside: Gandhi read the Gita's field as the human heart, and Krishna as the dweller within. Where did you notice two pulls in yourself? Day nine hundred fifty-eight.

A woman plants a row of mango saplings at the edge of a village. She may not be living there when the first fruit comes, and somebody else's children will climb those branches. She waters them anyway, every evening, carefully, as if the harvest were hers. Is that foolish, or is it the whole point? When Gandhi made his own Gita in Gujarati, he didn't name it after Krishna or after the battle. He named it after one idea, and that idea is the shape of what she's doing. Today, the word on the cover.
screen: `SHE PLANTS FOR A HARVEST SHE MAY NOT SEE.` → `SHE WATERS THEM ANYWAY.` → `THE WORD ON THE COVER.`

segments.voice: The title is Anasakti Yoga. Anasakti is usually put into English as non-attachment, or selfless action: doing the work without clinging to what it gets you. Gandhi said this was the Gita's central teaching, the one the rest of the book circles around. The idea is gathered in a verse in the second chapter, where Krishna tells Arjuna, in paraphrase: your right is to the work alone, never to its fruits. Don't let the fruit be your reason for acting. And don't cling to doing nothing, either. That last part matters. The verse closes the easy exit. Letting go of the fruit is not the same as walking away from the field. Here Gandhi pushes against a misreading. Non-attachment, he wrote, does not mean not caring how things turn out. The one who lets go of the fruit is not careless. That person is wholly given to doing the task well, because nothing is being saved up for the reward. Attention that would have gone to the prize goes into the work itself. Gandhi had a picture for this elsewhere in his writing, in a little book called Hind Swaraj. The means, he said, are like a seed, and the end is like a tree. You can't plant one kind of seed and expect another kind of tree. So if you care about the end, care first about the means, because the means are the part actually in your hands. Put the two ideas side by side and the mango planter makes sense. She can't make the tree bear on her schedule. She can water it well tonight. Anasakti is that evening watering, done with full care, while the harvest is let go.
screen: `ANASAKTI: NOT CLINGING TO THE FRUIT.` · `YOUR RIGHT IS TO THE WORK ALONE.` · `LETTING GO IS NOT NOT CARING.` · `THE MEANS ARE A SEED, THE END A TREE.` · then, large: `WATER IT WELL TONIGHT.`

segments.voice: Settle, and let the breath find its own pace. Pick one thing you're working on right now: a project, a conversation you're hoping goes well, a person you're trying to help. Notice how much of your mind is already standing at the finish line, waiting for the result. Gently walk it back to the part that's actually in your hands today. One small step. See yourself doing just that step, with care. On each out-breath, set the result down, the way you'd set down a bag you've been carrying. If you pray, you can offer the work, and its fruit, to Krishna, or to the one you pray to. The bell holds the time.
Gandhi's Gita. He called it Anasakti Yoga: the work given fully, the fruit let go.
Your line: Gandhi's Gita. Today, do one task as if no one will ever thank you for it, and do it well anyway. Water the tree. Day nine hundred fifty-eight.

959.title: Gandhi's Gita
959.hook: how does a person of steady wisdom walk?
959.howItsDone: Some Hindus learn the closing verses of the Gita's second chapter, on the person of steady wisdom, by heart and recite them as a daily reading.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the word on the cover of Gandhi's Gita: anasakti. The work given fully, the fruit let go, the tree watered anyway. What did you do today that no one will thank you for? Day nine hundred fifty-nine.

How does a wise person walk? It sounds like a riddle, but it's Arjuna's real question, near the end of the Gita's second chapter. Krishna has just been describing a person whose understanding is steady, and Arjuna wants specifics. What are the marks of such a person? How do they speak? How do they sit? How do they walk? It's a down-to-earth question. Krishna's answer is the portrait we met three days ago, the one Gandhi kept coming back to. Today we read it slowly, on the last of our days with Gandhi's Gita.
screen: `HOW DOES A WISE PERSON WALK?` → `ARJUNA WANTS SPECIFICS.` → `THE PERSON OF STEADY WISDOM.`

segments.voice: The Sanskrit name for this person is sthitaprajna, one whose wisdom stands firm. Krishna's portrait comes in a run of verses, and here they are in paraphrase. Such a person is content in the Self alone. Sorrow doesn't shake them, pleasure doesn't grab them, and they are free of craving, fear and anger. Then comes the first image: like a tortoise drawing in its limbs, this person can draw the senses back from the things that pull at them. Not destroying the senses. Drawing them in, when needed. Krishna doesn't pretend this is easy. A person who simply goes without, he says, may keep away from the things they want, but the taste for them stays behind. Only when the highest is seen does even the taste fall away. Then a stranger picture. What is night for all beings, the self-controlled one is awake in. And what everyone else is awake to is night for the one who sees. Two people in the same room, keeping different hours. The portrait ends with the sea. Rivers pour into the ocean all the time, and the ocean stays full and unmoved. So, Krishna says, is the one into whom desires flow without disturbing them. That one finds peace. Look back over these days and you can see why Gandhi held the passage close. On his reading, the Gita's battlefield is the heart. Anasakti is how to work on that field without clinging to the fruit. And the sthitaprajna is what a person looks like after long practice: still walking, still speaking, still in the world, but steady, like the sea.
screen: `STHITAPRAJNA: WISDOM THAT STANDS FIRM.` · `LIKE A TORTOISE DRAWING IN ITS LIMBS.` · `THE TASTE STAYS BEHIND.` · `RIVERS POUR IN; THE SEA STAYS STILL.` · then, large: `STEADY, LIKE THE SEA.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let your hands rest. Try the tortoise. Notice the senses one at a time: the sounds in the room, the light on your eyelids, the feel of the chair, any smell in the air. Don't push them away. Just, one by one, draw your attention back from each, the way a tortoise draws in a foot, until what's left is the breath. If something pulls you back out, a thought of something you want, notice that the taste for it is still there, and let it sit without following it. Then picture the sea: rivers coming in, the water staying level. If you pray, you can rest in Krishna, or in the one you pray to, as the still water. The bell holds the time.
Gandhi's Gita. The heart as the battlefield, anasakti as the way to work, and the person of steady wisdom, unmoved like the sea, as the goal.
Your line: Gandhi's Gita. Today, when a screen, a smell or a sound pulls at you, draw in once like the tortoise, then come back out on purpose. Day nine hundred fifty-nine.

fork.setup: you're Arjuna. Krishna has been praising a person of steady wisdom. you want to know what such a person is actually like. what do you ask?
options: what such a person believes about the gods.
how such a person speaks, sits and walks.

fork.reveal: Arjuna asks for the marks: how they speak, sit and walk. Krishna's answer is the portrait Gandhi kept close: content in the Self, drawing in like a tortoise, still like the sea.

original.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: kurma, tortoise, the image of Gita 2:58 for drawing the senses in.

trapdoor: what you thought: a wise person is someone who knows a lot.
what it means: in the Gita, the person of steady wisdom is someone desire can pour into without moving them, like the sea.
what a scholar hears: Arjuna's question in 2:54 is practical, how such a person speaks, sits and walks, and Krishna's answer closes the Gita's second chapter.

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 2:54–72 (Arjuna's question; the tortoise, 2:58; the taste that stays, 2:59; night and waking, 2:69; the sea, 2:70)
